detail.title: Principle-Based Marketing: A Theory and Conceptual Model
detail.abstract: Organisations face persistent challenges integrating socially responsible practices with marketing strategy, often resulting in consumer scepticism, inconsistent benefits, and implementation failure. While corporate social responsibility (CSR) and cause-related marketing (CRM) literature extensively outlines what to do, it provides insufficient guidance on how to effectively conceptualise, apply and measure these aspirations. In response, the theory of principle-based marketing (PBM) is presented, providing a novel consumer-centric framework grounded in fundamental organisational principles. By synthesising insights across multiple marketing schools of thought, theories of corporate conduct, and evolving socially driven marketplace dynamics, PBM bridges the gap between broad CSR mandates and measurable marketing practices. The theory is applied in practice with a proposed process model delineating the relationships among five key factors (Objective Commitment, Cognisance, Communication, Internal Congruence, and External Congruence) to deliver organisational marketing outcomes. The paper offers theoretical contributions through integrative systems thinking and provides managers with an organisational typology to strategically assess risks, position their brand, and audit their portfolio to align with socially driven norms and CSR imperatives.

detail.title: Leveraging Extensive Linguistic Models for Enhanced Business Process Management: An Exploratory Research Agenda
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the potential of advanced linguistic models to transform business process management (BPM) research and practice. It identifies key opportunities for integrating these models into the BPM lifecycle, with a focus on how they can enhance process analysis, design, and execution. Through an exploratory research approach, the paper outlines a set of research questions and proposes a future research agenda aimed at addressing the challenges and realizing the benefits of applying linguistic models in business management contexts. The paper contributes to the development of theoretical frameworks and practical guidelines for the utilization of these emerging technologies in BPM.

title: Content Creation Under Reward Income Fluctuations
affiliations: , University of Southern California - Marshall School of Business and University of Southern California - Marshall School of Business

detail.title: Content Creation Under Reward Income Fluctuations
detail.abstract: Independent content creators can face highly volatile reward income that fluctuates across periods, yet little is known about how this volatility affects their content production decisions. This paper studies how both reward income levels and their fluctuations influence creators' content production choices. We develop a "learning to learn" model where creators learn how their income is predicted from their own content creation and consumption experiences. Using data from a leading Chinese livestreaming platform, we find that income fluctuations substantially reduce creator welfare by an amount equivalent to approximately one-fourth of average reward income. We also document significant gender differences in risk preferences and find that COVID-19 lockdowns affected creators' risk attitudes. These effects persist when we extend our model to include both monetary rewards and non-monetary engagement metrics. To mitigate the effects of volatile reward income streams, we propose an income smoothing policy that adjusts platform's commission rates to stabilize creators' earnings over time. Our counterfactual simulations demonstrate this approach could simultaneously increase platform revenue, encourage more content production, and enhance content variety.

title: Gender Inequality And Household Purchase Decisions: The Case of Automobiles in China
affiliations: University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management, University of Toronto, Rotman School of Management and National University of Singapore (NUS)

detail.title: Gender Inequality And Household Purchase Decisions: The Case of Automobiles in China
detail.abstract: How do major social shifts like rising gender equality alter high-stakes household consumption? As women’s economic power grows, their influence over joint purchases like automobiles increases, yet causal evidence on how this shapes market outcomes remains scarce. This paper investigates how a fundamental dimension of gender equality—the education gap—affects household car purchases, a major financial decision in the Chinese auto market. Using administrative data on 15 million new vehicle registrations, we first document that female ownership is significantly higher in more gender-equal regions. To establish causality, we leverage the staggered rollout of China’s 1986 Compulsory Schooling Law as a natural experiment, which exogenously reduced the gender education gap with varying intensity across regions and birth cohorts. Our instrumental variable analysis provides novel causal estimates: closing the gender education gap by one year increases the probability of a car being registered to a woman by a substantial 9.6 percentage points. This effect is strongest for higher-priced, foreign-brand sedans, suggesting a genuine shift in control over the primary family vehicle, not just secondary ones. Corroborating this shift in influence, we also find that a smaller education gap increases the market share of female-preferred vehicle attributes (e.g., color), even for cars ultimately registered to men. Our findings offer key insights for firms, demonstrating that rising gender equality is not just a social trend but a fundamental driver of market evolution that reshapes demand for high-value goods.

title: Tools, Techniques, and Applications of Data Visualization in Education and Machine Learning

detail.title: Tools, Techniques, and Applications of Data Visualization in Education and Machine Learning
detail.abstract: Data visualization (DV) and learning analytics (LA) play a critical role in simplifying complexity, enhancing interpretation, and supporting evidence-based decision-making across educational, business, healthcare, and policy domains. Despite the rapid growth of research between 2015-2025, gaps remain in methodological transparency, tool adoption, and balanced reporting of advanced visualization techniques. This review systematically examines DV and LA literature to (i) assess trends in publication outputs and geographical contributions, (ii) identify the most frequently applied databases, tools, and visualization techniques, (iii) analyze decision-making outcomes and cognitive load implications, (iv) map target user groups, and (v) highlight persistent challenges and limitations constraining the field. A systematic search of Google Scholar, Scopus, and Web of Science yielded 101,685 initial records. After duplicate removal and screening, 123 studies were included for full analysis. Studies were classified into categories of visualization tools, techniques, application domains, and decision-making outcomes. Descriptive statistics and thematic synthesis were applied, and results are reported with visual summaries. Research outputs show steady growth with peaks in 2021-2024, dominated by journal articles (69.92%) and contributions from the United States (24.39%), China (18.70%), and India (10.57%). The most frequently used databases were Google Scholar (52.03%), Scopus (30.08%), and Web of Science (17.89%). Tool distribution highlighted the dominance of Tableau (44.72%), Power BI (14.63%), and Excel (8.94%), while dashboards (26.83%), bar graphs (16.26%), and line graphs (12.20%) were the most reported visualization techniques. Education (43.09%) and business (39.84%) emerged as the leading domains of application, with decision-making outcomes most often improving business/industry performance (30%) and policy or healthcare (15% each). Cognitive load findings revealed a balance between reduction strategies (25%) and risks of complexity (20%), underscoring design trade-offs. User groups were led by analysts (32.52%), managers (19.51%), and researchers/students (17.07% each). Key limitations included complexity and scalability (20%), interpretability issues (18%), and data integration challenges (15%). The evidence demonstrates that DV and LA provide significant pedagogical, operational, and strategic benefits. However, reliance on dashboards and descriptive methods reflects underutilization of advanced predictive or interactive approaches. Addressing methodological transparency, scalability, and user training will be essential for broader adoption. A framework (Figure 18) is proposed to integrate inputs, context, methods, mechanisms, users, and boundaries, offering a structured path toward advancing the role of DV and LA in educational decision-making.

title: Experimentation in Online Advertising
affiliations: University of Maryland - Robert H. Smith School of Business and University of Washington - Michael G. Foster School of Business

detail.title: Experimentation in Online Advertising
detail.abstract: Online advertisers face a critical challenge in measuring incrementality, the true lift in conversions attributable to advertising. While randomized controlled trials (RCTs) provide the most credible estimates, they entail fixed implementation costs and opportunity costs from holdouts. We develop a game-theoretic model analyzing the strategic interactions between advertisers and ad platforms where advertisers must conduct costly experiments to learn ad incrementality. Our analysis yields three main insights. First, ex ante symmetric advertisers may adopt asymmetric experimentation strategies, with some forgoing experimentation despite its high informational value. Second, the platform's reserve price serves a novel strategic role beyond surplus extraction by shaping advertisers' incentives to experiment. Third, ad platforms may strategically deter experimentation, despite efficiency gains from advertiser learning, to avoid the opportunity costs from holdouts. We provide new theoretical insights into the economics of ad experimentation and offer managerially relevant implications for both advertisers' and platforms' strategies in online advertising markets.

publicationDetails.detailsText: FRB of New York Staff Report No. 1166
publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of New York Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper studies how individuals sort into entrepreneurship and invention-related occupations and how their interactions shape innovation and economic growth. We develop an endogenous growth model in which occupational sorting jointly determines the supply of R&D talent and entrepreneurs' demand for it. Empirically, using Danish microdata, we show that transformative entrepreneurs-those who hire R&D workers-tend to have higher IQ and education and build faster-growing firms than other entrepreneurs. Quantitatively, the estimated model indicates that financial barriers to education misallocate talent; alleviating them through education subsidies increases both demand and supply of R&D workers, raising innovation and long-run growth. Broad startup subsidies are ineffective.

title: Gadget Promotion and Usage: Adverse Effects on Health and Psychological Well-Being of the Young Generation
affiliations: , Stamford University Bangladesh and Stamford University Bangladesh - Department of Business Administration

detail.title: Gadget Promotion and Usage: Adverse Effects on Health and Psychological Well-Being of the Young Generation
detail.abstract: This study examines the impact of excessive gadget promotion and peer pressure on the gadget usage behavior of youth and evaluates the long-term physical and psychological effects of digital overreliance. The research utilizes data from 500 respondents aged 12 to 26 in urban Bangladesh and using Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) to analyze the relationships among critical variables, such as marketing exposure, social comparison, and digital engagement. The results indicate that promotional material substantially elevates screen time and impulsive buying behaviors in youngsters. Extended usage of electronic devices is linked to several negative physical consequences, including eye strain, sleep disruptions, and persistent fatigue, with psychological impacts such as increased anxiety, reduced self-esteem, and increased social comparison. Furthermore, peer pressure and social impacts are identified as mediators that strengthen the connection between promotional stimuli and device utilization. The research emphasizes the urgent necessity for digital well-being programs and education on appropriate technology utilization. This research contributes to the growing discourse on youth digital well-being by providing a South Asian perspective and offers significant insights for educators, lawmakers, parents, and technology developers aiming to alleviate the negative effects of excessive gadget use.

title: The Unequal Motherhood Penalty: Maternal Preferences and Education
affiliations: and University of Sheffield

detail.title: The Unequal Motherhood Penalty: Maternal Preferences and Education

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: We study how maternal preferences interact with education to shape the motherhood penalty. Using rich Finnish registry data and the quasi-random gender of the firstborn child, we show that mothers across education groups display a mild preference for daughters, reflected in their fertility and parental leave choices. Yet this shared preference translates into divergent long-run outcomes. Ten years after birth, highly educated mothers face a 10% larger earnings penalty if their firstborn is a son, whereas less educated mothers experience slightly higher penalties with daughters. These differences stem from distinct labor market adjustments: less educated mothers are marginally more likely to exit employment after having a daughter, while highly educated mothers with daughters disproportionately move into public-sector jobs, which offer a relative wage premium. Our findings demonstrate that similar parental preferences can generate contrasting long-term earnings dynamics across education groups, highlighting the role of maternal preferences and labor market sorting in shaping the motherhood penalty.

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence and Internationalisation: Opportunities and Challenges for Australian Higher Education

publicationDetails.detailsText: University Development and Administration - Trends, Internationalization and Regional Developments in Higher Education 2025

detail.abstract: This chapter presents a reflective and critical commentary on the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into the internationalisation strategies of Australian higher education. Drawing on existing literature, relevant policy frameworks, and illustrative examples of documented practice, it examines how AI is reshaping classrooms, student recruitment and support, collaborative research, and knowledge exchange. While AI offers significant potential to enhance inclusivity, efficiency, and the global reach of Australian universities, it also raises ethical, governance, and equity challenges, including risks of data privacy breaches, algorithmic bias, and digital inequality. The chapter argues that AI adoption must be guided by principles of fairness, transparency, and partnership, ensuring technology complements rather than replaces human and intercultural dimensions of international education. It highlights the need for robust governance aligned with national standards, participatory policymaking involving diverse stakeholders, and sustained commitment to equity in global engagement. The discussion concludes with recommendations for context-sensitive, ethical, and inclusive AI integration, providing a conceptual foundation for future research and responsible implementation.

title: Impact of Digital Infrastructure on Supply Chain Robustness: The Mediating Role of Risk Mitigation
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Impact of Digital Infrastructure on Supply Chain Robustness: The Mediating Role of Risk Mitigation
detail.abstract: This study investigates how digital infrastructure, encompassing management information systems and digital supply chains, affects supply chain robustness, with a specific focus on the mediating influence of risk mitigation practices. Data from 360 employees in Saudi Arabian textile firms was analyzed using structural equation modeling. The results indicate a significant positive relationship between digital infrastructure capabilities and supply chain risk mitigation, and between risk mitigation and supply chain robustness. Furthermore, supply chain risk mitigation partially mediates the relationship between digital infrastructure and supply chain robustness, highlighting its crucial role in enhancing resilience. The findings underscore the importance of investing in digital infrastructure and strengthening risk mitigation strategies to foster more robust supply chain operations.

detail.abstract:
Purpose-This study aims to explore how a firm's exposure to economic policy uncertainty (EPU) affects the use of fair value (FV) measurement for non-financial assets. 

Design/methodology/approach-The analysis focuses on the selection of FV models for different types of non-financial assets. It examines how internal factors and external policy shocks (EPU) influence the adoption of FV measurement through regression analyses. 

Findings-The results reveal that firms with greater sensitivity to EPU are significantly less likely to adopt FV accounting for non-financial assets. This tendency is especially pronounced among firms that benefit from uncertain environments and is consistent with the conservatism principle. The effect varies by firm characteristics and industry context-being more evident among larger firms, those with high tangible assets or volatile cash flows and those operating in regulated or non-real estate sectors. 

Originality/value-This study contributes to the literature by linking macroeconomic uncertainty to accounting policy choice, highlighting EPU as a key external determinant of FVadoption. It extends prior work focused on internal drivers by empirically documenting how firms adapt accounting practices in response to policy uncertainty.

title: Algorithmic Trauma Bonds: Conditioning Dependency in Digital Labor Markets
affiliations: The Job Applicant Perspective

detail.title: Algorithmic Trauma Bonds: Conditioning Dependency in Digital Labor Markets

declarations.ethicsApproval: This paper is a more academic white-paper version of a blog post meant to academically stake claim to the concept. I have used AI in the editing and the ordering of references, but all ideas contained within are fully my own and my responsibility.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces the concept of algorithmic trauma bonds, describing how digital platforms in hiring and dating reproduce the psychological dynamics of trauma bonding at scale. In personal relationships, trauma bonds emerge when the same source inflicts harm and provides intermittent relief. Behavioral economics has shown that such intermittent reinforcement, particularly on a variable-ratio schedule, produces the strongest persistence of behavior. Digital platforms mirror this logic. Job seekers may face dozens of ghost postings or automated rejections, only to receive a sudden "top candidate" notification or interview request. Daters may be ignored repeatedly, only to be pinged with "Someone liked you!" The unpredictability sustains engagement. Critically, platform revenues grow not from resolution (a hire or a stable match) but from retries, reposts, boosts, and churn. Revelio Labs data shows the hires-perposting ratio fell from ~0.75 in 2018 to <0.5 in 2023, while Bureau of Labor Statistics data shows a flat hires rate despite rising postings. Recruit Holdings reports rising revenue per paid job ad even as ad volume fell. These outcomes demonstrate that inefficiency is not accidental but incentivized. By monetizing dependency, platforms create algorithmic trauma bonds that prolong unemployment and erode trust.

title: A Unified Fluid Model for Large Service Systems with Patience- or Delay-Dependent Service Times
affiliations: , Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST), Northwestern University - Kellogg School of Management and Southern Methodist University (SMU)

detail.title: A Unified Fluid Model for Large Service Systems with Patience- or Delay-Dependent Service Times
detail.abstract: We consider queueing systems with a large agent pool, assuming the service time of each customer depends on the delay of that customer in queue. Such dependence can be due to the customers having patience for waiting that depends on their individual service requirement, or due to having their service-time distribution being a function of the time spent in queue. We refer to the former dependence mechanism as exogenous and to that latter as endogenous. Since exact analysis of the stochastic system under either dependence mechanism is intractable, we propose a deterministic approximation of the (mean) queueing dynamics, and refer to that approximation as a Unified Fluid Model (UFM) since it captures both dependence mechanisms simultaneously. When the arrival rates and staffing levels are constant, we characterize conditions for the existence of a unique stationary point for the UFM, and prove that those conditions always hold when the dependence is exogenous. In the endogenous-dependence case, the UFM may possess multiple equilibria, with each equilibrium point being either locally stable, so that any trajectory of the UFM passing in a neighborhood of that point will converge to it, or unstable, so that any trajectory is “repelled” from that point (unless initialized at that point). The implications for the stochastic system of the UFM having multiple equilibria are twofold: First, the stochastic fluctuations may be an order of magnitude larger than the typical fluctuations in many-server systems. Second, the system may experience congestion collapse, namely, become substantially more congested than it should be under the current staffing level and arrival rate.

detail.abstract: The National Volume-Based Procurement (NVBP) is a recent policy implemented by the Chinese government to improve the affordability of medical treatments. The program covers a wide range of therapeutic classes, including anti-infective, oncology, and neurological drugs, with price reductions reaching up to 74.5% in 2024 (PhIRDA, 2024). This paper analyzes the potential impact of introducing significantly cheaper procured drugs on the prices of branded and locally distributed generic alternatives. The result suggests that under consumers' heterogeneity, the price effect is ambiguous; therefore, a minimum procured amount is required to achieve meaningful health expenditure savings. Using a lagged dependent model and machine learning-based statistical methods, I estimate a policy effect of a 20-97 RMB annual reduction in health expenditure per capita, equivalent to a 1.1%-5.6% reduction in 2020 spending level. These findings also provide insights for the US government negotiating prices with drugs after the price protection period under Inflation Reduction Act, highlighting broader implications for government strategies in pharmaceutical markets.

detail.abstract: A recurring question in the mortgage default literature is why underwater default is rare relative to model predictions. We find that one answer is miscalibration of flow payoffs. We build a novel, detailed quantitative model of mortgage default and find that realistic rent dynamics plus mild levels of default costs are sufficient to eliminate negative-equity strategic default. We present further empirical results supporting our model's focus on flow payoffs. Our model addresses the underwater mortgage default puzzle, offers more realistic interpretations of policy consequences, and reinforces the theoretical effectiveness of cash-flow-based interventions.

detail.abstract: We conduct mean comparison tests and regression analyses on a sample of 65 countries to explore the structural and cultural determinants of national R&D investment. We find a legal effect whereby structural drivers are effective only under a strong rule of law. Cultural openness and long-term orientation also show positive associations with R&D investment. While innovation efficiency attracts foreign R&D, innovation efficacy deters it, as profitable opportunities are usually exploited by domestic investors. Moreover, we identify a substitution effect in which governments offset insufficient domestic and foreign investment. Our findings have policy relevance, as we highlight underexplored enhancers of R&D beyond the usual financial or cost-related factors, providing new insights for designing more effective innovation and research strategies.

detail.abstract: This paper documents that during the late 20th Century, nominal government bonds and stocks tended to comove positively, whereas during the first quarter of the 21st Century they have tended to comove negatively. A similar sign switch is observable for real government bonds and breakeven inflation rates. Recent macroeconomic events have caused short-lived changes in these comovements, and periods with high risk premia tend to be periods in which bond-stock comovements are large in absolute value. The paper surveys theoretical models of these phenomena.

detail.abstract:
Purpose-We used difference-indifferences research design to investigate the effect of the outbreak of extreme environmental events near firms' headquarters on the cost of debt.

Design/methodology/approach-Using a sample of Chinese firms listed on the Shanghai and Shenzhen A-Share markets from 2004 to 2020, we find that treated firms, those that have extreme environmental events occurring within 25 kilometers of their headquarters, have a higher cost of debt. 

Findings-We find an increase in the cost of debt for firms headquartered in areas where local environmental events occur, suggesting that the outbreak of extreme environmental events strengthens local government's environmental enforcement and supervision. 

Originality/value-Our paper contributes to the emerging literature on the role of environmental risk and performance in the context of debt financing. We extend prior literature on the determinants of the cost of debt from the perspective of the exogenous extreme environmental events.

title: AI in Retail Banking
affiliations: Dresden University of Technology and Dresden University of Technology

detail.title: AI in Retail Banking
detail.abstract: Retail banking serves as the primary interface between the financial system and society, making advances in artificial intelligence (AI) highly visible and seemingly disruptive. This article synthesizes numerous publicly communicated bank use cases, recent academic research, and insights from expert interviews to systematize current and anticipated AI developments in retail banking. While these changes may appear abrupt to customers, they largely follow a logical progression when viewed through the perspective of finance, information systems, and management science. We observe a convergence of these previously separate research domains, driven by increasing customer orientation and service-centric approaches. Across use cases, the trend is toward highly personalized, comprehensive services-a "family office for everyone"-paired with efforts to support do-it-yourself financial management. To advance future research, scholars must adopt interdisciplinary perspectives that integrate the technical and broader social science dimensions of AI in retail banking.

detail.title: Geopolitical Risks, Inflation Pressure, and the U.S. Treasury Yield Curve
detail.abstract: The U.S. Treasury yields reached a 20-year high under acute inflation pressure in the post-pandemic era amid aggravated geopolitical conflicts. To quantify the underlying effects of regional geopolitical risks (GPRs) of key U.S. strategic interests, we employ an extended affine term structure model with unspanned GPRs and conventional macroeconomic drivers. We find that GPR shocks, particularly those manifesting U.S.-China rivalry, contribute more to expectations and variations of inflation and yields than shocks to U.S. macroeconomic variables. The results warn on the adequacy of monetary policy in curbing inflation in a fragmented global order with escalating GPRs.

title: The Battle for Historical Truth: How Cultural Institutions Counter Radical Incrementalism

detail.title: The Battle for Historical Truth: How Cultural Institutions Counter Radical Incrementalism

detail.abstract: This paper examines the systematic assault on American cultural institutions through the lens of "radical incrementalism"-a strategy that achieves comprehensive reform through seemingly small, incremental steps. Focusing on the Trump administration's 2025 executive orders targeting institutions like the Smithsonian, this analysis reveals how anti-woke rhetoric operates as sophisticated historical revisionism designed to erase marginalized communities' contributions from national memory. The study documents specific cases including Executive Order 14253 "Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History, " which mandates removal of "divisive" content from federal cultural institutions, and the termination of grants to museums like the Whitney Plantation. Through examination of contemporary policy implementation alongside historical patterns of cultural erasure, the paper demonstrates how digital amplification, economic interests, and legal challenges intersect to threaten historical education and institutional independence. Drawing on theoretical frameworks from political science and cultural studies, the analysis argues that current efforts to control historical narratives follow international patterns of authoritarian revisionism while exploiting uniquely American vulnerabilities around race and national identity. The paper concludes with strategic recommendations for cultural institutions to resist systematic historical erasure through legal frameworks, coalition building, and public education initiatives. This research contributes to understanding how democratic institutions can preserve historical truth against coordinated political assault.

detail.abstract: Myogenic differentiation factor 1 (MyoD1) protein regulate the development of skeletal muscle in the host. Mutated MyoD1 can cause rhabdomyosarcoma and thus is deemed one of the important cancer biomarker. Non-human primate MyoD1 proteins are important reference to that of the human MyoD1 protein in gene editing therapies. In this study, we consolidated all 31 primate MyoD1 and characterized them in terms of phylogenetic and proteomic. All primate MyoD1 proteins are generally highly indifferent in terms of motif distribution and protein secondary structure. The Philippine tarsier outstands the others in terms of isoelectric point, motif distribution and phylogenetic tree. The data yielded from this study can be used to foster and enhance future MyoD1-associated disease and cancer therapies.

title: Next-Gen Frontiers in Veterinary Anaesthesia and Analgesia: Integrating AI, CRISPR, Microbiota, Music, and Botanicals
affiliations: University of Malaysia Sarawak

detail.title: Next-Gen Frontiers in Veterinary Anaesthesia and Analgesia: Integrating AI, CRISPR, Microbiota, Music, and Botanicals
detail.abstract: Veterinary anaesthesia is entering a transformative era, driven by advancements in AI, CRISPR, microbiome research, sensory stimulation, and botanical science. This review explores the emerging synergies between traditional anaesthetic methods and futuristic technologies. AI is enhancing anaesthesia monitoring, CRISPR enables custom genetic models to refine protocols, and the gut-brain axis influences anaesthetic sensitivity. Additionally, the calming effects of music and low-frequency vibrations, alongside the therapeutic use of herbal sedatives, are offering low-impact alternatives for stress and pain management. These interdisciplinary integrations could revolutionize anaesthetic safety and efficacy in animals. We propose a holistic view of anaesthesia that balances pharmacologic precision with biologically and environmentally responsive techniques.

title: Creating Lasting Influence by Biased News Media on the Swing Voter's Decision
affiliations: Dongguk University and Kyung Hee University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Creating Lasting Influence by Biased News Media on the Swing Voter's Decision

declarations.declarationOfInterest: We declare that we have no relevant or material financial interests related to the research described in this paper.

detail.abstract: We consider a monopolistic, biased news media platform that attempts to influence the decision of swing voters with cheap talk when voting is costly and abstaining is an option. First, we demonstrate that, while no fully communicative equilibrium exists in a stage game, a partially truth-revealing mixed-strategy equilibrium exists. In this equilibrium, the platform occasionally releases biased news, and the swing voter either follows it or abstains with a positive probability. We also characterize a partially revealing equilibrium in infinitely repeated games where the platform's information distortion is monitored either perfectly or imperfectly ex post after voting, and where the swing voter is not sufficiently patient. Notably, repeated interactions do not lower the platform's steering probability in the case of perfect monitoring. However, they lower the probability that the swing voter will abstain. In both the perfect and imperfect monitoring cases, a mixed-strategy equilibrium in which the swing voter transitions to the punishment phase with a positive probability can enhance efficiency, akin to what is observed in a stage game. Our results provide a probable explanation for the persistence of biased news media.

title: Evaluation and intervention to improve show rates in a pediatric neurology clinic
affiliations: Indiana University Purdue University Indianapolis (IUPUI) - Indiana University School of Medicine, Indiana University Purdue University Indianapolis (IUPUI) - Indiana University School of Medicine, Indiana University Purdue University Indianapolis (IUPUI) - Indiana University School of Medicine and Indiana University Purdue University Indianapolis (IUPUI) - Indiana University School of Medicine

detail.title: Evaluation and intervention to improve show rates in a pediatric neurology clinic
detail.abstract: Patient access is one of the greatest issues in healthcare today.  Pediatric neurology is a specialized field with a significant shortage in providers, which means that wait times can be several months in duration.  Patients who miss appointments without calling to cancel or reschedule are called “no-shows.”  No-shows lead to further delays in patient access as those visit slots go unfilled.  With this study, we evaluated risk factors for patients who no-show appointments, put into place an intervention for patients found to be at high risk for no-showing, and evaluated the effects of this intervention.  The intervention consisted of clinic schedulers calling the patient’s parent or guardian directly to remind them of their appointment.  Families were then given the option to keep, cancel, or reschedule their appointment.  The intervention resulted in improved show rates among high-risk patients, improved patient access, and a 32% increase in clinic revenue.

title: Financial Literacy and Household Financial Resilience
affiliations: Beijing Technology and Business University - Business School, Beijing Technology and Business University, University of Hull and Beijing Technology and Business University

detail.title: Financial Literacy and Household Financial Resilience
detail.abstract: Rising uncertainty has drawn researchers' attention towards households' anti-risk capacities. Using data from the China Household Finance Survey covering 2019 to 2021, this study investigates the impact of financial literacy on household financial resilience. We measure household financial resilience by analyzing inter-period variations in liquid assets pre-and post-Covid-19, coupled with constructing a sensitivity index. Our analysis indicates that financial literacy significantly enhances financial resilience through the wealth effect and risk mitigation effect. This study highlights the critical role of financial literacy in mitigating risks and accelerating recovery from financial disturbances.

title: Sustainability Labels vs. Reality: How Climate-friendly are Green and ESG Funds?
affiliations: , Banque de France, European Central Bank (ECB) and Bank of England, European Central Bank (ECB)

detail.title: Sustainability Labels vs. Reality: How Climate-friendly are Green and ESG Funds?

publicationDetails.journalName: ECB: Working Paper Series (Topic)

detail.abstract: This paper assesses the environmental performance of sustainability-related investment funds compared to conventional ones across three dimensions: financed activities, portfolio carbon footprint, and investment in firms with ambitious science-based targets. We identify ESG funds using Morningstar (MS) strategies, the Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation’s Article 8/9 classification, and funds’ self-naming. We find that the greenest funds invest more in low-carbon sectors, but their carbon footprints are comparable to conventional funds. Also, MS Low-Carbon and Art.8 funds tend to invest in the same sectors as conventional funds but target less polluting firms. Overall, results reveal inconsistencies between ESG labels and outcomes, highlighting the limited role these funds currently play in financing the transition to a net-zero economy.

title: What Can Newspaper Articles Reveal About the Euro Area Economy?
affiliations: and European Central Bank (ECB)

detail.title: What Can Newspaper Articles Reveal About the Euro Area Economy?

publicationDetails.journalName: ECB: Working Paper Series (Topic)

detail.abstract: This study introduces a novel approach to dictionary-based sentiment analysis that extracts valuable insights from economic newspaper articles in the euro area without requiring article translation. We develop sentiment indices that accurately measure economic, labour, and inflation perceptions in Germany, France, Italy, and Spain using native-language texts. The aggregation of these country-specific sentiments provides a reliable indicator for the euro area as a whole, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach in several nowcasting and forecasting experiments. This translation-free method significantly reduces resource requirements, facilitates easy replication across various languages, and enables daily updates. By eliminating the translation bottleneck, our approach emerges as one of the most timely and cost-effective economic measures available, offering a powerful tool for monitoring and forecasting business cycles in the multilingual context of the euro area.

title: The local supply effect of asset purchases: Evidence from the Eurosystem’s Corporate Sector Purchase Programme
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and De Nederlandsche Bank - Monetary and Economic Policy Department

detail.title: The local supply effect of asset purchases: Evidence from the Eurosystem’s Corporate Sector Purchase Programme
detail.abstract: We estimate to what extent the Eurosystem’s Corporate Sector Purchase Programme (CSPP) impacted the price of securities that were actually bought, or their close substitutes, more than the price of other securities. For own bond purchases we do not find such local supply effects, which is in line with the Eurosystem’s market neutrality principle of asset purchases. We do, however, find significant local supply effects caused by the purchases of substitute bonds defined by similar maturities; we estimate that these effects reduce bond yields by about 40-45 basis points. These effects are more pronounced for bonds that were eligible under the CSPP than for non-eligible bonds, for bonds that have been issued more than a year ago and for bonds with relatively low credit ratings.

title: Firms’ National Spirit and Green Innovation
affiliations: Jiangnan University, National Taipei University, National Chiao Tung University and National Taipei University

detail.title: Firms’ National Spirit and Green Innovation
detail.abstract: In this paper, we examine the effect of the firms’ rhetorical national spirit on corporate green innovation in China. We find that firms with stronger rhetorical national spirit have higher levels of green patenting. To establish causality, we employ the instrumental variable approach and exploit the US-China trade war as an exogenous shock. Greener policy environments, Competitive markets, state-owned enterprises, and the CEO’s greater awareness of environmental issues strengthen this positive relationship. Using China’s green credit guidelines and a path analysis, we further show that firms with stronger rhetorical national spirit tend to abide by national green policies and do not follow national policies only rhetorically. As a reward, these firms enjoy lower taxes and an increased chance of securing government procurement contracts due to their green investments.

title: The Effects of Minimum Wage Increases on Poverty and Food Hardship
affiliations: University of Oxford, , Bocconi University and University of California, Berkeley

detail.title: The Effects of Minimum Wage Increases on Poverty and Food Hardship

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: We study how minimum wage (MW) increases affect poverty and food hardship in the United States from 1981 to 2019. Applying stacked difference-in-difference models and the Supplemental Poverty Measure (SPM), we find that a $1 MW increase reduces poverty by 0.3 to 0.7 percentage points among all working-age adults, and by 1.2 to 1.7 percentage points among individuals most likely to work in MW jobs.  We also find that a $1 MW increase reduces food insufficiency by 1.5 percentage points among likely-MW workers. Effects on poverty are partially offset by higher living costs in MW-increasing states.  Our findings are robust across methodological choices that have divided the recent literature. Overall, MW increases meaningfully reduce poverty and food hardship for the workers most directly affected and deliver modest improvements for the broader working-age population.

title: Effects of Team Diversity on Individual Performance and Voice: A Field Experiment of Group Composition by Gender and Language
affiliations: London School of Economics, University of Sheffield, Yale University and

detail.title: Effects of Team Diversity on Individual Performance and Voice: A Field Experiment of Group Composition by Gender and Language

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: We present results from a field experiment that tests the effects of varying gender and linguistic group composition on performance and on group-members' perception that their voice is heard when completing complex collaborative work within a low scrutiny environment. We randomize individuals enrolled in a postgraduate course populated by mostly women and non-native English speakers into small teams within larger, exogenously assigned seminar groups. Groups are tasked with complex and deliberative research assignments over three months. Using administrative and survey data, we find that a higher share of women in seminar groups significantly benefits the academic performance of group members—an effect driven by a positive effect on female native English speakers—while a greater proportion of women in small teams improves non-native language speakers' perception of being heard.

title: Covariate Balancing and the Equivalence of Weighting and Doubly Robust Estimators of Average Treatment Effects
affiliations: Brandeis University - Department of Economics,  and Michigan State University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Covariate Balancing and the Equivalence of Weighting and Doubly Robust Estimators of Average Treatment Effects

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: How should researchers adjust for covariates? We show that if the propensity score is estimated using a specific covariate balancing approach, inverse probability weighting (IPW), augmented inverse probability weighting (AIPW), and inverse probability weighted regression adjustment (IPWRA) estimators are numerically equivalent for the average treatment effect (ATE), and likewise for the average treatment effect on the treated (ATT). The resulting weights are inherently normalized, making normalized and unnormalized IPW and AIPW identical. We discuss implications for instrumental variables and difference-in-differences estimators and illustrate with two applications how these numerical equivalences simplify analysis and interpretation.

title: The Impact of Neighbour, Colleague, and Family Peers on Parental Labour Supply
affiliations: Leiden University and Erasmus University Rotterdam (EUR) - Department of Economics

detail.title: The Impact of Neighbour, Colleague, and Family Peers on Parental Labour Supply

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: Child penalties in paid working hours are persistent and widen the gender earnings gap. This paper studies an important mechanism through which working hours are affected: peer effects. Using three unique layers of peer networks: neighbours, colleagues, and family, we analyse peer effects on individuals' paid working hours. We analyse peer effects up to six years after childbirth on individuals who become first-time parents in the period 2014-2018, using Dutch full-population administrative monthly microdata up to September 2024. The identification strategy exploits exogenous variation in peers' working hours through peers-of-peers. Our research is the first to establish long-term statistically significant peer effects on fathers' working hours. The results indicate positive peer effects on fathers and mothers, where colleague peers are more important than neighbour peers and family peers.

title: Multigenerational Inequality
affiliations: Charles III University of Madrid

detail.title: Multigenerational Inequality

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: A growing literature provides evidence on multigenerational inequality  the extent to which socio-economic advantages persist across three or more generations. This chapter reviews its main findings and implications. Most studies find that inequality is more persistent than a naive iteration of conventional parent-child correlations would suggest. We discuss potential interpretations of this new "fact" related to (i) latent, (ii) non-Markovian or (iii) non-linear transmission processes, empirical strategies to discriminate between them, and the link between multigenerational and assortative associations.

title: The Inherent Nonlinearity in Learning: Implications for Understanding Stock Returns
affiliations: Kellogg School of Management - Department of Finance, Yale School of Management and Northwestern University

detail.title: The Inherent Nonlinearity in Learning: Implications for Understanding Stock Returns

publicationDetails.detailsText: FRB of Chicago Working Paper No. 2025-16
publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Financial markets (and more generally the real economy) display a wide range of important nonlinearities. This paper focuses on stock returns, which are skewed left—generating crashes—and have volatility that moves over time, is itself skewed, is strongly related to the level of prices, and displays long memory. This paper shows that such behavior is actually almost inevitable when prices are formed by investors acquiring information about the true, but latent, value of stocks. It studies a general model of filtering in which agents receive signals about the fundamental value of the stock market and dynamically update their beliefs (potentially with biases). When those beliefs are non-normal and investors believe crashes can happen, prices generically display the range of nonlinearities observed in the data. While the model does not explain where crashes come from, it shows that investors believing that prices can crash is sufficient to generate the rich higher-order dynamics observed empirically. In a simple calibration with i.i.d. shocks to fundamentals, the model fits well quantitatively, and regression-based tests support the model’s mechanism.

reference: FRB of Chicago Working Paper No. 2025-17
title: The Decline of the Variance Risk Premium: Evidence from Traded and Synthetic Options
affiliations: Kellogg School of Management - Department of Finance and Yale School of Management

detail.title: The Decline of the Variance Risk Premium: Evidence from Traded and Synthetic Options

publicationDetails.detailsText: FRB of Chicago Working Paper No. 2025-17
publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Equity index options historically displayed sharply negative returns and CAPM alphas. This could reflect investor risk preferences or intermediary frictions. We document that over the past 15 years, option alphas have become indistinguishable from zero. We also introduce synthetic options, that, under some conditions, reflect risk preferences of the average equity investor, independent of option-market frictions. Synthetic options never, over the last 100 years, had negative alpha, indicating that equity investors never required high compensation for market downturns. An intermediarybased model explains the patterns in both synthetic and traded options, including the recent decline in the variance risk premium.

title: Public Payment Mandates and Provider Supply
affiliations: Georgia State University - Andrew Young School of Policy Studies, Georgia State University - Andrew Young School of Policy Studies and

detail.title: Public Payment Mandates and Provider Supply

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: Public insurance reimbursement policies shape the structure and reach of healthcare markets. In this study, we examine the 1980 federal Medicaid mandate requiring states to reimburse Certified Nurse-Midwives, one of the first reforms targeting non-physician providers. We find the mandate increased midwife-attended deliveries by 1.1 percentage points, an 80% rise, adding about 1,100 midwife births annually per state by 1985. We also document a geographic expansion of midwife services into unserved areas and increased hospital employment, consistent with supply-side labor market responses. Our findings demonstrate that reimbursement mandates directly alter healthcare delivery by expanding provider use and reshaping the workforce.

reference: Boston Univ. School of Law Research Paper Forthcoming
title: The Fed, Offices as Property, and the Meaning of "Cause"
affiliations: Boston University - School of Law

detail.title: The Fed, Offices as Property, and the Meaning of "Cause"

publicationDetails.detailsText: Boston Univ. School of Law Research Paper Forthcoming
publicationDetails.journalName: Boston University School of Law Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
The Federal Reserve Act states that "each member shall hold office for a term of fourteen years from the expiration of the term of his predecessor, unless sooner removed for cause by the President." 12 U.S.C. § 242. Based on the historical record, when Congress creates an office with a fixed term of years and protects against removal without "cause," Congress has both granted "a constitutionally protected property interest" under the Fifth Amendment (that cannot be taken away without "due process") and extended a statutory entitlement to receive fair notice and a meaningful opportunity to respond before any removal may take effect. 

Constitutional Protection: Under English law through the eighteenth century, termed executive offices-even cabinet-level offices-were considered "freehold" property, subject to protections from removal akin to those applicable to real property. This conception-of termed offices as "property"-would have been well known to the Founders and was reflected in Founding-era documents and commentary. The Constitution was drafted with this understanding. 

Statutory Protection: Independent of the Fifth Amendment, the "cause" requirement has a long-established common law meaning of requiring notice and an opportunity to be heard before removal. This understanding hails from pre-Founding English common law, and it is likewise reflected in American precedents soon before Congress drafted the Federal Reserve Act of 1913. The Act’s text of “cause” should be read in this context.

“Faithful Execution.”  Article II of the Constitution requires the President to undertake a “faithful execution” of the laws.  From a historical perspective, there is nothing inconsistent with that obligation and recognizing procedural protections for employees who can be terminated only for cause.

title: Gender Identity Norms, Mental Health, and Relationship Strain
affiliations: Monash University - Centre for Health Economics, Monash University and

detail.title: Gender Identity Norms, Mental Health, and Relationship Strain

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: Although studies have evaluated the costs of violating the male breadwinner norm, little is known about the mental health consequences, particularly for common conditions such as depression and anxiety. We explore this issue using Australian national administrative tax and healthcare records. We estimate individual- and employer-level fixed models of mental health service use and prescription medication. We find that men are significantly more likely to use mental health care following periods when their wife earns more, with the strongest effects emerging two years after the earnings shift. By contrast, we find no consistent effects for women. Our results are robust to alternative specifications, including the inclusion of controls for labour market shocks, and an alternative estimation strategy based on a local linear regression discontinuity design. We find that couples are also more likely to separate following norm violations, suggesting relationship strain as a key mechanism. Complementary evidence on relationship satisfaction from Australian household survey data provide further support of this pathway. Our findings demonstrate that traditional gender identity norms impose psychosocial costs within modern households.

title: Modal Split Perceptions and Preferences for Public Funding
affiliations: RWI - Leibniz Institute for Economic Research

detail.title: Modal Split Perceptions and Preferences for Public Funding

publicationDetails.journalName: United States Association for Energy Economics (USAEE) & International Association for Energy Economics (IAEE) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Using data from a 2024 survey among 3,052 participants in Germany, this study looks at the modal split indicator from the perspective of laypersons. This indicator is often used to communicate local mobility goals with the public. We investigate whether people are able to guess the modal split distribution in their locale, which modal split would be ideal in their view, and how these perceptions influence opinions on public spending for transportation. We also examine whether showing examples of real modal splits to a random subset of participants influences accuracy or any of our other markers. Results indicate that participants have some trouble guessing modal split proportions, and that the examples did not significantly improve this. For example, only 17% of participants' guesses for the car share are within 5 percentage points of the real split. However, 85.6% of participants would like the share of car trips to be lower by on average 22.2 percentage points (mean perceived car share is 55.2%). Additionally, introducing people to the concept of the modal split without also giving real world reference points negatively influences the amount of public funds they would like to be assigned to sustainable transportation modes.

title: The effects of open banking on fintech providers: evidence using microdata from Spain
affiliations: Banco de España, Banco de España, CUNEF Universidad and Banco de España

detail.title: The effects of open banking on fintech providers: evidence using microdata from Spain

publicationDetails.detailsText: Banco de Espana Working Paper No. 2514
publicationDetails.journalName: Banco de Espana Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Open banking initiatives, which aim to increase competition and innovation in the financial sector by enabling the customer-authorised sharing of financial data among banks, regulated third-party providers and other financial stakeholders, are becoming widespread around the world. This paper investigates the impact of open banking on the development of the fintech sector, focusing particularly on payment-related financial services. We utilise the implementation of the Second Payment Services Directive (PSD2) in Europe as a natural experiment and employ a difference-in-differences methodology to analyse a unique microdata set of 406 Spanish fintech firms from 2014 to 2022, sourced from the Banco de España Central Balance Sheet Data Office and Fintech Radar. Our findings reveal that following PSD2, fintech firms specialising in payment services (Paytech) improved their performance compared with non-payment fintechs (control), with this improvement driven primarily by revenue growth rather than cost reduction. Additionally, treated fintech firms exhibited a significant reduction in long-term bank debt reliance, securing more stable market-equity funding. We also find that Paytech firms increased their liquidity holdings, reduced their labor intensity while increasing their labor costs and enhanced their productivity. Our results contribute to the literature on open banking by providing empirical evidence of its benefits for fintech firms, particularly in the payment sector, and underscore the importance of regulatory frameworks in fostering innovation and competition. These insights are valuable for policymakers aiming to enhance financial sector dynamics through data-driven regulations.

title: The Economics of Data for Generative AI: Trade-offs and Optimal Copyright Policy
affiliations: University of Lausanne - Faculty of Business and Economics (HEC Lausanne)

detail.title: The Economics of Data for Generative AI: Trade-offs and Optimal Copyright Policy
detail.abstract: We propose a welfare lens for copyright and AI training that separates two needs: broad access to the existing stock of works and a steady flow of new works to keep models fresh. Royalties can fund that flow but also raise prices and add administrative cost. We compare four regimes: AI exception with opt-out, AI exception with opt-out, a licensing market, and a new policy option: statutory licence. Our results suggest that a statutory licensing regime can be optimal. When a modest royalty can reliably fund the creation needed to keep data fresh, a statutory licence tends to deliver the highest welfare by combining full coverage with sustained flow. If that funding is unrealistic or administrative cost is high, zero-royalty baselines (exception or opt-out) perform better. Opt-in restores funding but sacrifices coverage; opt-out can come close to statutory when coverage is already near full. Calibration and simulations support a simple rule for practice: target the smallest royalty that restores freshness, keep administrative cost low, and monitor outcomes.

title: Climate Change Exposure: Does CSR Committee Quality Matter?
affiliations: University of Otago, University of Otago, University of Otago and University of Otago - Department of Accountancy and Finance

detail.title: Climate Change Exposure: Does CSR Committee Quality Matter?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflicts of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: This work was supported by a University of Otago Doctoral Scholarship.

detail.abstract: Using a manually constructed multidimensional board-level specialized CSR committee quality index of S&P 500 firms from 2014 to 2022, we examine the impact of firm-specific CSR committee quality on firm-level climate change exposure. Drawing on stakeholder and agency theories, we find that higher CSR committee quality reduces climate change exposure. We further investigate the underlying mechanism and document that the main effect is more pronounced in firms with higher eco-innovation and greater nature dependence. In addition, the main impact is more substantial following the 2016 Paris Accord ratification and among firms headquartered in the non-swing and Democratic-leaning states. We also show that firms with effective CSR committees mitigate climate change-related transition and regulatory shocks. Our findings imply that effective CSR committees enhance resilience against climate risk exposure. Cross-sectional analyses reveal that the negative association between CSR committee quality and climate risk exposure is stronger for firms that are younger, have lower managerial ability, and have higher institutional ownership. Collectively, our study underscores the importance of CSR committee quality in driving responsible business practices, leading to better management of firm-level climate change-related vulnerability. Our findings are robust to alternative measures of primary variables and endogeneity concerns.

reference: GWU Legal Studies Research Paper 2025-50; GWU Law School Public Law Research Paper 2025-50
title: Policy Brief:  The Federal Banking Agencies Should Withdraw Their Deeply Misguided Proposal to Weaken Leverage Capital Requirements for the Largest U.S. Banks
affiliations: George Washington University Law School

detail.title: Policy Brief:  The Federal Banking Agencies Should Withdraw Their Deeply Misguided Proposal to Weaken Leverage Capital Requirements for the Largest U.S. Banks

publicationDetails.journalName: George Washington University Law School Legal Studies Research Paper Series

publicationDetails.detailsText: GWU Law School Public Law Research Paper 2025-50
publicationDetails.journalName: George Washington University Law School, Public Law & Legal Theory Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
On July 10, 2025, federal banking agencies issued a proposed regulation that would dangerously weaken capital requirements for the largest U.S. banking organizations.  The proposed rule would significantly reduce the enhanced supplementary leverage ratio (eSLR) requirements for U.S. global systemically important banking organizations (G-SIBs).  If adopted, the proposed rule would allow U.S. G-SIBs to become woefully undercapitalized, as their predecessors were at the outbreak of the global financial crisis of 2007-09.  The proposed rule would make U.S. G-SIBs highly likely to fail during future systemic financial crises, with catastrophic consequences for our financial system, economy, and society.  

As explained in this Policy Brief, the federal banking agencies should withdraw the proposed rule for the following reasons:

1. The proposed rule would contravene governing federal statutes, which require federal banking agencies to establish and enforce leverage capital requirements that are effective and binding components of capital standards for the largest U.S. banking organizations.

2. Strong leverage capital requirements are necessary to prevent large, complex banking organizations from taking excessive risks and manipulating risk-based capital rules to justify dangerously low levels of equity capital.

3. Federal bank regulators have permitted U.S. G-SIBs to reduce their leverage capital ratios to hazardously low levels by making excessive shareholder distributions, and the proposed rule would allow U.S. G-SIBs to become recklessly undercapitalized.

4. The proposed rule would expand “too-big-to-fail” subsidies for U.S. G-SIBs and undermine the competitive viability of community banks and regional banks, thereby reducing the availability of credit to consumers, farmers, and small businesses.

5. The proposed rule would increase the likelihood of a devastating systemic financial crisis by creating a sovereign-bank “doom loop,” in which the survival of U.S. G-SIBs would depend on the stability of the U.S. Treasury market and the credibility of the Federal Reserve System as monetary policy authority and lender of last resort.

title: The Global Network of Oligarch Companies
affiliations: University of North Carolina Kenan-Flagler Business School, Stanford Graduate School of Business, London Business School and University of Cambridge

detail.title: The Global Network of Oligarch Companies
detail.abstract: We study how Russian oligarch-affiliated companies operate globally and respond to sanctions. We construct a dataset tracking 71 companies, 1,800 international subsidiaries, and their institutional investors between 2009 and 2023. These companies maintain extensive networks, especially in tax havens. Difference-indifferences estimates show that the 2014 and 2022 sanctions had limited impact on the companies' global footprint or access to institutional minority investors. Instead, oligarch companies use more tax haven entities and withdraw from jurisdictions with beneficial ownership disclosure. Our findings highlight how organizational complexity and regulatory arbitrage undermine sanctions, suggesting that globally coordinated transparency regulation is critical for enforcement.

title: Pork Producers, Product Bans, and Petering Out Dormant Commerce Clause Extraterritoriality Inquiries

detail.title: Pork Producers, Product Bans, and Petering Out Dormant Commerce Clause Extraterritoriality Inquiries
detail.abstract: Constitutional commentary on the dormant Commerce Clause (DCC) reflects the Court's persistent failure to appreciate how the clause's contemporary application is problematic. The 2023 Pork Producers case was a propitious opportunity for the Court to resolve lingering issues, such as whether the DCC ought to include an inquiry into whether a subnational regulation produces impermissible extraterritorial effects, or whether the Pike v. Bruce Church balancing test remains an apt function for the judiciary. The Court squandered that opportunity, unfortunately. And this article examines how that transpired. It explores how product bans, such as the one adopted by California for humane treatment of pigs, enjoy a long lineage and absent intentional discrimination should avoid constitutional scrutiny under the DCC. When examining the fractured opinions in the case, it further suggests that the Court overlooks how both the extraterritoriality component of the DCC and the balancing test evolved and why they should be jettisoned in lieu of focusing on whether a subnational program involves intentional discrimination as a product of rent seeking behavior.

title: Modern Staggered Difference-in-Differences: From the Pitfalls of Two-Way Fixed Effects (TWFE) to Robust Estimation
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Modern Staggered Difference-in-Differences: From the Pitfalls of Two-Way Fixed Effects (TWFE) to Robust Estimation

detail.abstract: This document explains that the traditional Two-Way Fixed Effects (TWFE) model is flawed for staggered Difference-in-Differences (DID) analysis. detail.abstract: The persistent underinvestment in climate adaptation finance across emerging and developing economies (EMDEs) stems not only from real physical and financial risks, but from entrenched and misaligned perceptions of risk. Here we examine the adaptation finance gap in emerging markets and developing economies (EMDEs), emphasizing the disconnect between investor risk perception and the actual benefits of adaptation investment-with a focus on how such a disconnect can deepen the finance accessibility divide. The paper argues that the under-investment in adaptation finance is not only misplaced and inefficient, but actively dangerous-exacerbating fiscal fragility and cross-border cascading impacts. While real risks exist, their amplification through outdated macroeconomic models, limited financial return metrics, and inadequate policy signals has stalled investment. We argue that this distorted perception prevents necessary investment flows into climate resilience and adaptation infrastructure, particularly in countries most exposed to escalating climate impacts. The paper presents a new paradigm: one that reframes adaptation as a viable and urgent investment opportunity. This paper calls for recalibrating risk perception and establishing a coherent adaptation finance standard, using tools such as blended finance, policy signalling, and risk reallocation. As climate disasters increasingly affect global stability and security, this contributes to the urgent conversation around unlocking adaptation finance through systemic financial reform.

detail.abstract: Background and objective: This paper explores the likely evolution of federal and provincial excise revenues pursuant to the imposition of a second tranche of levies on vaping liquid in six of Canada's provinces that together account for 80% of the population. This serves as one anchor point for the analysis. The Canadian Tobacco and Nicotine Survey and the Canadian Community Health Survey furnish data on the consumer side. The Canadian Vaping Association has also supplied information on the product and value composition of the vaping market. These sources together facilitate a simulation approach to estimating market response and excise revenue. The imposition of additional levies on nicotine e-vapor products may unintentionally stimulate the market for combustibles. The excise levy should be modified. Simultaneously, the health and tax authorities could improve health-oriented decision making in the smoking and non-smoking populations by the provision of accurate information on risk and by using differential taxation as a signalling mechanism. detail.abstract: India is witnessing a decline in labor force participation alongside a rise in unpaid labor, particularly informal caregiving. While numerous studies document this broader trend, the specific caregiving contributions of middle-aged and older adults- particularly within multi-generational households- remain underexplored. Furthermore, the well-being effects of this often invisibilized labor remain poorly understood for this cohort, who are typically positioned as care recipients. Analyzing nationally representative data from the Longitudinal Ageing Survey of India (2017–19), this study shows that care provision adversely affects caregivers’ health, measured through health deficit accumulation using a frailty index. These results are robust across alternative specifications and estimation strategies. Heterogeneity analysis shows that the adverse effects are more pronounced among older, married, employed and urban female caregivers. The study underscores the need for policy interventions to expand formal long-term care systems and strengthen structured support for informal caregivers in India.

detail.abstract: This study investigates an analytics-driven approach to reproducing software defects that surface in production environments. We examine AISA (Automatic Issue Self-Analysis), a workflow that fuses user-journey analytics, application logs, and performance telemetry to infer minimal reproducible steps (MRS) for high-impact incidents. The research is organized around two questions: whether automation can reliably extract reproduction steps from production data and what challenges govern large-scale deployment. Using a mixed-method design-analytics mining on a production-like dataset with injected faults and expert evaluations by quality assurance (QA) and site reliability engineering (SRE) practitioners-we quantify AISA's ability to reconstruct failure paths, categorize incident classes, and reduce time-to-reproduction. Findings indicate that AISA surfaces frequent pre-error paths, highlights impacted users, and reduces manual debugging effort by more than half. The paper contributes by: (a) formalizing an evidence-centered session representation for reproduction, (b) specifying a pipeline that combines clustering, sequence modeling, and anomaly detection to synthesize deterministic replay steps, and (c) outlining governance controls for privacy, schema discipline, and auditability. We also provide advanced insights on data-driven automation in evidence curation, cross-layer test synthesis, and risk containment. These results contribute to advancing academic and practical discussions on production reliability engineering, model governance, and Genanalytics-driven software quality assurance.

detail.abstract:
Purpose-This paper examines the pricing effect of cross-sectional patterns in the cryptocurrency market, aiming to enhance the composition of asset pricing factors for a better explanation of cross-sectional variability in cryptocurrency returns.

Design/methodology/approach-The study utilizes data from 1,160 cryptocurrencies spanning over nine years, from January 2014 to December 2022, totalling 468 weeks. We obtain data for all cryptocurrencies using the application programming interface (API) provided by coinmarketcap.com and employ a well-established multifactor asset pricing methodology aimed at proposing an improved composition of cryptocurrency factors. 

Findings-The findings of the study uncover a strong size effect, a distinctive reversal effect, and a significant premium for cryptocurrency illiquidity. Contrary to the prevailing views, the observed reversal effect challenges the established momentum effect, while the observed illiquidity premium appears not to be explained by the size effect or other cross-sectional patterns. In response to these insights, the study introduces a novel four-factor asset pricing model, comprising the crypto market factor (CRm-Rf), crypto size factor (CSMB), crypto reversal factor (CLMW) and crypto illiquidity factor (CIHML). 

Originality/value-This paper contributes to the literature in three significant ways. Firstly, the comprehensive analysis of the cryptocurrency market from the perspective of empirical asset pricing enriches the available literature on cryptoasset pricing. Moving beyond the identified patterns of crypto market risk, crypto size effect and pervasive momentum effect in the market, our study advances the mostly used three-factor model with the reversal and illiquidity factors. The comparative evaluation of various combinations of three-factor, four-factor and five-factor models demonstrates the superior performance of the proposed four-factor model. Thirdly, the study identified a significant illiquidity premium in the cryptocurrency market.

detail.abstract: Did bank equity prices reflect growing sector imbalances before the 2023 failure of Silicon Valley Bank? We find that banks with higher reliance on uninsured deposits, or with higher marked-to-market leverage, had lower equity returns prior to SVB's collapse. Although markets priced uninsured deposits and high leverage individually, their interaction was not reflected in market prices prior to SVB’s failure. detail.abstract: In this essay, we outline how Health Artificial Intelligence (HAI) might impact health services and systems in resource-limited settings: we see the impact of HAI in the quantity, quality, cost, and range of health services available. AI provides an opportunity for resource-limited settings to develop and deploy context appropriate tools, allowing them to leapfrog existing challenges in health services delivery. An immediate impact of AI-enabled technology in health services in resource-limited settings is likely through an increase in the quantity of health services, where it might bring advanced clinical decision-making capacity to places where such services do not exist. Where they do exist, Health AI may improve the quality of services. And since the marginal cost of production of most software-enabled services tends to be minimal, these services could be scaled up cost-effectively. Health AI technologies may also provide health services that were not available before, thereby increasing the range of available services. In this essay, we elaborate on the above, providing specific examples where appropriate. We conclude by acknowledging the transformative potential of Health AI in resource limited settings, but challenges remain, not least of which is for these regions to become producers, and not just consumers, of scientific knowledge and technologies in Health AI.

detail.abstract: We investigate the impact of childbirth on the careers of women in innovation, a maledominated field. We find that the fertility rate of female inventors is remarkably low. Most female inventors have their first child only after filing their first patent application. Following birth, female inventors are much less likely to file patents. Much of the loss in patent output can be explained by temporary (maternity) leave, part-time work, and lower mobility. The innovation gap after childbirth leads to economically meaningful wage disparities, indicating a substantial depreciation of female inventors' human capital. Male inventors also face declines in their innovation output and earnings, but these losses are much smaller than those observed for women. Our findings emphasize the difficulties of reconciling a career in innovation with being a parent in general and with being a mother in particular.

This article applies a holistic conceptualization of sustainability to reflect critically on model assumptions and hence propose a list of 'sustainability features' covering social, ecological and economic factors including political, monetary, fiscal and temporal aspects.
